claim.statement: Claude Code Stop hook can inject content into the next turn by emitting JSON {decision:'block', reason:<text>}; the reason text becomes the next user-input the model sees.

evidence.summary: stop-hook.sh lines 181-188 emit jq -n '{decision:block, reason:$prompt, systemMessage:$msg}' which Claude Code interprets as do-not-exit and feeds reason as next user input.
Iteration 2 of this very session was triggered by exactly this mechanism. Live, end-to-end demonstration.

information_depth.rationale: Reference impl read end-to-end plus self-referential live demo.

claim.statement: The Claude Code model demonstrably reads injected content from a Stop-hook 'reason' field — current ralph iteration is acting on the validation prompt the hook injected, the strongest possible canary.

evidence.summary: If the model were not reading injected content, this validation work would not be happening — the only path that produced this turn is hook injection.

information_depth.rationale: Self-referential live proof.

claim.statement: Claude Code Stop hook receives session_id and transcript_path via stdin JSON, can read the full session JSONL transcript, and can extract the most recent assistant text block (text/tool_use/thinking are separate JSONL lines, all role=assistant).

evidence.summary: stop-hook.sh: line 32 reads session_id, line 68 reads transcript_path, line 98 greps role=assistant lines, lines 112-114 jq-extract text blocks. Production-grade impl.

information_depth.rationale: Reference impl complete.

claim.statement: Claude Code Stop-hook injection of 1.8KB prompt text via decision:block reason works without truncation. Ceiling above 1.8KB is untested. 10KB and 100KB tests still required.

evidence.summary: wc -c on /Users/jaredsmith/Projects/.claude/ralph-loop.local.md = 1815 bytes. Iteration 2 model received the prompt body intact — observed in this very turn.

information_depth.rationale: Single sample point. No upper bound established.

claim.statement: Claude Code hooks can be registered by either user settings (~/.claude/settings.json) or by a plugin's hooks/hooks.json. Plugin form supports ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} variable, enabling self-contained shell-script hooks. eyesd should ship as a CC plugin to get clean hook lifecycle.

evidence.summary: hooks.json shows the plugin pattern: {hooks:{Stop:[{hooks:[{type:command, command: 'bash ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stop-hook.sh'}]}]}}

information_depth.rationale: Pattern is in active use by ralph-loop plugin right now.

question.text: Does CC's UserPromptSubmit hook fire on every user turn, including programmatic input from /ralph-loop hook reinjection? Need a UserPromptSubmit hook that appends a UUID line to a log; submit N user prompts (interactive + -p headless), verify N entries; verify it also fires when content is injected via Stop hook decision:block.
question.resolution_criteria: Test in iteration 2: install a project-scoped UserPromptSubmit hook → run pi/codex/cc with deterministic prompt → grep log → confirm exactly 1 entry per submission.
question.why_it_matters: V1.1 is the architectural keystone. If UserPromptSubmit doesn't fire on hook-injected pseudo-user input, eyes architecture loses its 'observe user prompts' channel for CC.

question.text: What stdin payload does CC's UserPromptSubmit hook receive? Stop hook gets {session_id, transcript_path}. Does UserPromptSubmit also get the user's submitted prompt text directly (not just metadata)?
question.resolution_criteria: Install UserPromptSubmit hook with `command: cat > /tmp/upshook.json` → submit prompt with marker text → inspect /tmp/upshook.json for marker.

question.text: Where is codex CLI's hook configuration documented? `codex --help` shows no hook flags. ~/.codex/config.toml shows no [hooks] section. AGENTS.md asserts 'TOML-configured hook on UserPromptSubmit (and Stop), turn-scoped, behind a config flag' — find the feature flag and config schema.
question.resolution_criteria: Either: (a) find codex docs/release notes/source mentioning hook keys; (b) inspect codex binary strings for 'hook' references; (c) ask Anthropic/OpenAI directly. Validate by writing a test hook that prints a marker.
question.why_it_matters: Without this, codex falls back to MCP polling or .eyes/inbox.md — degrades architecture by one rung on the delivery-surface ladder.

question.text: What is pi's TypeScript extension lifecycle API? AGENTS.md says 'subscribing to input / before_* lifecycle events, injecting context into the next turn'. Installed extensions in ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ are providers + a colgrep tool — none are lifecycle-hook examples. Find the SDK type defs.
question.resolution_criteria: Locate pi extension SDK in /Users/jaredsmith/.nvm/versions/node/v22.14.0/lib/node_modules/pi/ (or wherever the npm package lives). Identify lifecycle event names. Write minimal index.ts that subscribes to input and writes to a log.

question.text: Do hooks fire in headless mode (claude-code -p / codex exec / pi -p)? Headless mode bypasses interactive UI; need to confirm the hook lifecycle is identical.
question.resolution_criteria: Run `claude -p 'hello' --append-system-prompt='...'` with a logged hook installed. Confirm log entry. Repeat for codex exec and pi -p.

question.text: What is end-to-end hook latency (hook fire → daemon → response → injection delivered)? Spec says sub-second. With no daemon yet, baseline is just hook-script execution time.
question.resolution_criteria: Hook script that records `date +%s%N` on entry and exit; subtract. Establish floor (no daemon round-trip) and ceiling (with stub daemon).

synthesis.title: L1 status after iteration 1
synthesis.summary: Claude Code hooks are substantially de-risked. V1.2/V1.3/V1.4 validated by reading ralph-loop's reference impl plus the live fact that this session is being kept alive by exactly that mechanism. V1.6 partial (1.8KB confirmed). V1.1, V1.5, V1.7, V1.8 still need explicit harness experiments. Codex and pi are ENTIRELY undemonstrated — discovery questions raised. Architecture decision implication: eyesd should ship as a CC plugin (not user-settings hook), to get ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} self-containment. The CC hook surface is firmly real and production-quality; this de-risks one of three first-party harnesses for v1.
synthesis.limitations: All L1 evidence so far is for claude-code only. Reference-impl evidence is strong but not a substitute for explicit canary tests. Codex hook config and pi extension SDK are still unknowns that block any concrete L1 work for those harnesses.

claim.statement: Codex CLI supports 8 canonical hook events as a stable feature: PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop. Configured via TOML in [hooks] section of config.toml or via plugin hooks.json. Three handler types: command (shell), prompt, agent. Schema matches Claude Code's hook format almost exactly: {hooks:{EventName:[{matcher,hooks:[{type,command,timeout,async,statusMessage}]}]}}.

evidence.summary: hook_config.rs HookEventsToml enum lists all 8 events as serde-renamed fields. Source-of-truth for the schema.
figma plugin hooks.json shows working PostToolUse hook with matcher 'Write|Edit' — same shape as CC.
hook_runtime.rs imports UserPromptSubmitRequest, PreToolUseRequest, etc. — runtime is real and wired up to the canonical events.

information_depth.rationale: Source-level schema definition + working plugin example. AGENTS.md was right: codex DOES support TOML hooks. The 'feature flag' mentioned is `features.hooks=true` which is stable+true by default per `codex features list`.

claim.statement: pi (TypeScript SDK) supports lifecycle events via pi.on(eventName, handler). Confirmed event names: 'input' (pre-prompt, returns {action: continue|transform|handled, text?}), 'session_start', 'session_shutdown' (post-stop), 'tool_call' (pre-tool), 'tool_result'. The 'input' handler receives {text, source} where source can be 'user' or 'extension' — pi natively distinguishes user vs extension-injected input, which is a freebie for V7.37 (mark watcher-originated content).

evidence.summary: extensions.md lifecycle table + Quick Start example showing pi.on('session_start',...) and pi.on('tool_call',...). Documents the full surface.
input-transform.ts: pi.on('input', async (event, ctx) => {...; return {action: 'transform', text: ...}}) — proves the 'input' event exists, has full prompt text, and supports rewriting.
auto-commit-on-exit.ts: pi.on('session_shutdown', ...) plus ctx.sessionManager.getEntries() to read full transcript — proves V1.4 path for pi.

information_depth.rationale: Documentation + 70+ working examples in pi's repo. APIs are a TypeScript SDK, not shell hooks — fundamentally different ergonomics from CC/codex but functionally equivalent.

claim.statement: Codex hooks can inject context into the next turn via a ContextInjectingHookOutcome. Both UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart hooks return outcomes that get converted into context-injecting outcomes — the hook can append additional context the model sees alongside (or instead of) the user's prompt.

evidence.summary: hook_runtime.rs: 'impl From<SessionStartOutcome> for ContextInjectingHookOutcome' and 'impl From<UserPromptSubmitOutcome> for ContextInjectingHookOutcome' — explicit type conversions show the hook output is structured for context injection.

information_depth.rationale: Type-level evidence is strong; haven't yet read the conversion bodies to know exactly how the injected context appears in the model's input (system message? user message prefix? separate block?). Need to test empirically.

claim.statement: pi 'input' event handler can transform user input text before the LLM sees it by returning {action: 'transform', text: <new_text>}. This is full text replacement, not append. For 'append context' semantics, an extension would either prepend/append within the transform string OR push entries via ctx.sessionManager. Question still open whether append-style injection (vs full text replace) is supported.

evidence.summary: input-transform.ts line 27: 'return {action: "transform", text: `Respond briefly in 1-2 sentences: ${query}`};' — full replacement. The 'handled' action skips the LLM entirely.

information_depth.rationale: Replacement is proven; append-only injection (the eyesd architecture's preferred mode) needs further investigation in pi's session-entry API.

claim.statement: All three first-party harnesses support hooks but with three different ergonomics models: (a) Claude Code: shell-command hooks, JSON via stdin, JSON-decision via stdout, registered in user settings or plugin hooks.json. (b) Codex CLI: shell-command OR prompt OR agent hooks, TOML config in ~/.codex/config.toml or plugin hooks.json. (c) pi: TypeScript SDK, in-process callbacks, returns action+payload object. CC and codex have nearly identical config formats — eyesd can ship one hooks.json template that works for both. pi requires a separate TS extension. The 'eyesd-as-CC-plugin' decision generalizes: ship hooks.json for CC+codex, ship a .ts extension for pi.

evidence.summary: codex hook_config.rs schema.
codex figma plugin hooks.json — identical shape to CC plugin hooks.json.
pi extensions.md — TS SDK, fundamentally different shape.

information_depth.rationale: Three reference impls compared head-to-head.

claim.statement: pi's input event payload includes event.source which natively distinguishes 'user' input from 'extension' input. This means V7.37 ('Injected content clearly marks itself as watcher-originated') is solved for pi at the harness level — eyes-injected text via an extension call would carry source='extension' and any other extension's input handler can react accordingly. CC and codex do not have this distinction natively; eyesd must add explicit content markers (e.g., wrap in <eyes:WATCHER_NAME>...</eyes>) for those harnesses.

evidence.summary: input-transform.ts line 17: 'if (event.source === "extension") { return {action: "continue"}; }' — source field exists and is checked.

information_depth.rationale: Direct API evidence.

claim.statement: Claude Code hooks fire by default in headless mode (claude -p). The --bare flag explicitly disables hooks (along with LSP, plugin sync, etc.) — this confirms hooks are otherwise active in non-bare modes including --print. The --include-hook-events flag adds hook lifecycle events to the stream-json output for inspection.

evidence.summary: --bare doc string: 'Minimal mode: skip hooks, LSP, plugin sync...' — implies hooks are on by default. --include-hook-events doc: 'Include all hook lifecycle events in the output stream (only works with --output-format=stream-json)'.

information_depth.rationale: Documentation evidence; haven't run a headless canary yet.

question.text: What is the exact JSON schema codex hook commands write on stdout to inject context (vs CC's {decision:'block', reason:<text>})? Need to read the conversion-body of impl From<UserPromptSubmitOutcome> for ContextInjectingHookOutcome in hook_runtime.rs to determine the wire format.
question.resolution_criteria: Read hook_runtime.rs lines containing the From<*Outcome> impls; OR write a test hook that returns various JSON shapes and observe codex behavior.

question.text: Per-harness injection size ceiling: 1KB / 10KB / 100KB. CC has 1.8KB confirmed. Codex and pi entirely untested. Hook stdin/stdout pipes have OS-level buffer limits (typically 64KB on macOS pipe). For codex's prompt/agent handlers (not just command), size limits may differ.
question.resolution_criteria: Write a fixture hook for each harness that injects N KB of marker text where N in {1, 10, 100, 1000}. Confirm round-trip through grep on transcript / next prompt.

question.text: Codex hooks have an `async: bool` flag. What's the latency model? Sync hooks block the model turn until they return; async hooks fire-and-forget. For eyesd: watcher results MUST come back to the model turn, so the user-facing hook must be sync. But the hook itself just talks to eyesd via socket — the watcher work is already done in the background. So sync hook + non-blocking eyesd query == still sub-second. Verify this works: test a sync command hook that calls a fast unix-socket lookup.
question.resolution_criteria: Build a test hook that does `nc -U /tmp/test.sock` and measure round-trip. Should be <50ms for tiny payloads.

synthesis.title: L1 status after iteration 2 — all 3 harnesses confirmed to support hooks
synthesis.summary: All three first-party harnesses have real, documented hook surfaces. CC and codex use nearly-identical TOML/JSON config formats with shell-command hooks; pi uses TypeScript SDK with in-process event handlers. AGENTS.md was correct on all three points. Architectural risk for L1 (the 'keystone') is now LOW — there is no harness-level blocker to building eyesd. Open work for full V1.* validation: empirical canary tests for each harness (UserPromptSubmit fires, payload contains text, content lands in next turn). Plus size ceiling tests for V1.6 and headless tests for V1.7. The 'eyesd ships as CC plugin + codex plugin + pi extension' approach is now concrete: the same hooks.json template covers CC and codex.
synthesis.limitations: All evidence is documentation/source-level. No empirical canary tests run yet. The conversion bodies in codex's hook_runtime.rs (how injected context appears in the model input) still need close reading. Pi's append-vs-replace question for input event still open.

acquisition.details: `rg --files` listed only CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, docs/, knb/, and bead metadata. `rg -n "eyesd|daemon|pidfile|socket|SIGINT|SIGTERM|pending message|cursor"` found only documentation and existing knb rows; no source tree, CLI, daemon binary, runtime, or tests exist yet.

claim.statement: V2.9 is blocked: no eyesd daemon implementation exists yet. Passing requires a project-scoped daemon start path that writes a pidfile for the running process and refuses a second daemon for the same project.

qualifiers.passing_criteria: Start eyesd in an isolated project; observe a live process and pidfile; run start again and observe a clear refusal without spawning a second process.
qualifiers.test_fixture: Temporary project with a deterministic runtime dir. Start daemon once, inspect pidfile and process table, start again, assert only one daemon PID exists and the second command exits nonzero or returns a structured already-running status.
design_questions: What defines daemon identity: canonical project root, git worktree root, explicit --project path, or runtime socket path?
Where should pidfile/socket/state live so multiple projects and multiple harness sessions do not collide?

evidence.summary: docs/validation.md item 9 defines the required behavior: starts cleanly, writes a pidfile, refuses double-start.
AGENTS.md states the project is pre-implementation and v1 scope includes the eyesd daemon.
Repo inventory shows no daemon source, CLI, runtime, or tests exist yet, so the behavior cannot be validated empirically.

information_depth.rationale: The validation requirement is clear and the absence of implementation is directly observed; final semantics depend on daemon design.

claim.statement: V2.10 is blocked: no eyesd daemon or watcher supervisor exists yet. Passing requires the daemon to survive a child watcher crash, keep accepting requests, and keep sibling watchers isolated.

qualifiers.passing_criteria: A watcher subprocess can exit nonzero, panic, time out, or be killed without terminating eyesd or corrupting the daemon's queue/status state.
qualifiers.test_fixture: Temp project with two watcher profiles: one deliberate crash watcher and one healthy echo watcher. Trigger a tick, assert eyesd PID remains live, the crash is recorded once in status, the healthy watcher still returns a parseable message, and hook polling still works.
design_questions: Does eyesd restart crashed long-lived watchers or spawn watchers per tick?
How are crash statuses exposed without spamming the working agent on every tick?

evidence.summary: docs/validation.md item 10 requires eyesd to survive a watcher crash.
AGENTS.md defines watchers as secondary agents invoked by eyesd and states watchers never edit code.
Repo inventory shows no daemon, watcher supervisor, or lifecycle tests exist yet.

information_depth.rationale: The required failure boundary is explicit; supervisor model and reporting policy remain design choices.

claim.statement: V2.11 is blocked: no eyesd signal handling or socket lifecycle exists yet. Passing requires clean SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown that stops watchers, flushes durable state, closes the Unix socket, and removes the socket path.

qualifiers.passing_criteria: On SIGINT and SIGTERM, eyesd exits within a bounded time, leaves no live child watchers, persists required queue/cursor state, and removes its socket path so a restart can bind cleanly.
qualifiers.test_fixture: Start eyesd in a temp project, create at least one queued message and one child watcher, send SIGTERM in one run and SIGINT in another, then assert process exit, no child leak, socket path removed, state file readable, and immediate restart succeeds.
design_questions: What exit code/status should a signal-driven graceful shutdown report?
Which resources must be flushed synchronously before exit vs best-effort?

evidence.summary: docs/validation.md item 11 requires clean SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown and socket removal.
AGENTS.md identifies the Unix socket as the watcher-to-daemon transport and the daemon as the bus.
Repo inventory shows no signal handler, socket owner, daemon process, or cleanup tests exist yet.

information_depth.rationale: Behavior is specified at validation level; exact shutdown contract still needs implementation design.

claim.statement: V2.12 is blocked: no eyesd state store exists yet. Passing requires pending message queue state and per-delivery-channel cursors to persist across daemon restarts without message loss or duplicate delivery.

qualifiers.passing_criteria: After restart, queued watcher messages, monotonic message IDs, and delivery cursors are restored exactly; polling returns only messages newer than each channel cursor.
qualifiers.test_fixture: Temp project with two channels or sessions. Enqueue messages 1..N, advance cursor for only one channel, restart daemon, assert persisted queue/cursor state, then poll both channels and verify one sees only new messages while the other still sees its pending backlog.
design_questions: What storage format should eyesd use for durable state: JSONL, SQLite, sled, or another embedded store?
Are delivery cursors scoped by harness session, project, watcher, delivery surface, or some composite key?

evidence.summary: docs/validation.md item 12 requires pending message queue and per-channel cursor state to persist across daemon restarts.
AGENTS.md message delivery design depends on pending messages and cursor-like polling/injection behavior.
Repo inventory shows no durable state implementation or restart tests exist yet.

information_depth.rationale: The persistence requirement is explicit; storage and cursor identity are unresolved design choices.

claim.statement: V2.13 is blocked: no eyesd socket owner or startup recovery path exists yet. Passing requires startup to distinguish a stale socket left by a dead daemon from a live daemon's socket, remove only stale paths, and then bind cleanly.

qualifiers.passing_criteria: If the previous daemon died ungracefully and left a socket path behind, next start recovers automatically; if a live daemon owns the socket, next start refuses as V2.9.
qualifiers.test_fixture: Create an orphan socket/file in the runtime dir or kill -9 a test daemon, then start eyesd and assert cleanup plus successful bind. In a separate run with a live daemon, assert double-start refusal and no socket removal.
design_questions: How should eyesd prove a socket is stale: connect probe, pidfile check, lockfile, or a combination?
How should it handle non-socket files at the expected socket path?

evidence.summary: docs/validation.md item 13 requires stale-socket recovery after ungraceful daemon death.
AGENTS.md makes the Unix socket the watcher-to-daemon channel, so socket recovery is part of daemon lifecycle.
Repo inventory shows no socket owner, stale-socket probe, or startup recovery tests exist yet.

information_depth.rationale: The recovery behavior is specified; stale-vs-live detection strategy is an implementation decision.

question.text: What is the canonical eyesd runtime identity and runtime directory? L2 startup, pidfile, socket cleanup, and stale-socket recovery all depend on whether identity is the canonical project root, git worktree root, explicit --project path, or socket path.
question.resolution_criteria: Before implementing V2.9/V2.11/V2.13, choose one identity rule and document the runtime path layout. Validation fixture should then derive pidfile/socket/state paths from that same rule.
question.why_it_matters: Without a stable identity rule, double-start refusal, multi-session routing, and stale-socket recovery can contradict each other.

question.text: What durable store should eyesd use for pending messages, monotonic IDs, and per-channel cursors?
question.resolution_criteria: Pick a storage format and durability contract before V2.12 implementation. The chosen store must support crash-safe append/update, exact cursor restoration, and simple inspection in validation fixtures.
question.why_it_matters: State persistence is the bridge between L2 daemon lifecycle and L7 message deduplication. A weak store will create duplicate or lost watcher messages after restart.
